Search found no directly matched 2024–2026 study establishing gains for a lightweight, randomly initialized title/description encoder jointly trained with GRU4Rec under this four-category protocol. Recent related approaches often violate the pretrained-weight constraint: [CALRec (2024)](https://research.google/pubs/calrec-contrastive-alignment-of-generative-llms-for-sequential-recommendation/) uses PaLM-2 and multi-category pretraining; [title–content matching (2024)](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7390/12/13/2125) uses BERT and combines content and collaborative predictions. An older, relevant precedent, [Ask the GRU (2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02116), trains a GRU text encoder end-to-end through recommendation supervision and reports improved cold-start scientific-paper recommendation. Its auxiliary metadata task helps sparsity, but its setting does not establish sequential Amazon benchmark gains.

A constraint-compatible hypothesis is one GRU4Rec network with item representations formed from jointly learned ID embeddings plus a gated text residual. Start with random token embeddings, separate masked mean pooling for titles and truncated descriptions, and a small projection; test a shallow text CNN only if pooling helps. Feed the same representations into the history GRU and candidate scoring so text receives next-item supervision throughout. These are proposed adaptations, not demonstrated results. Shared words could help sparse items, while generic descriptions could blur item identity; retain ID embeddings and tune text strength/dropout. Compare ID-only, title-only augmentation, and title-plus-description augmentation sequentially within the GPU budget, selecting solely by fixed macro validation HR@10. No retrieved source supports a numerical gain or runtime estimate for this exact protocol.
